studies.title: Your Efforts Run Apart
studies.meaning: Three oaths that are all pairs: night and day, one covering and one uncovering, and then the making of male and female. The claim they support is about divergence. Your strivings are scattered, going in different directions, which is the natural conclusion from a creation built out of opposites. Then the surah begins sorting, and the first of the two types is defined by three things, one of them giving.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and early. The surah goes on to describe two men in opposite directions, one who gives and one who withholds, and the classical sources connect the later ayat to particular individuals in Mecca, though the reports differ over who is meant. These opening lines carry no occasion. They set up the sorting with three pairs drawn from the sky and the body.

keyTerms.note: A verb for something spread over a thing until it is hidden, used of a cloth laid on a body. The night is described as an action rather than as an absence of light.
The particle can mean what or who, and scholars differ here. Most read it as naming the Creator, some as naming the act of creating itself, and the ambiguity is recorded rather than resolved.
A plural adjective for things going different ways, used of camels dispersing to graze. It says the directions differ rather than that some are better, and the sorting comes in the next line.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Herds went out at first light and scattered across the grazing, each animal taking its own line, and by evening they had to be gathered again. The word the surah uses for human efforts is the word for that scattering. A listener who had spent mornings watching a flock disperse across a valley would have had the picture before the argument arrived.
studies.didYouKnow: The two types described after this passage are given in matching shapes: three conditions each, then a promise built on the same verb. One is eased toward ease, the other eased toward hardship. The Quran uses the identical word for both, which means the same process is described running in two directions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The oaths make difference structural. Night and day, male and female: creation is built out of opposed pairs, and human effort is placed in the same category. That normalises divergence before any judgement is passed, so the sorting that follows is not a complaint about variety but a claim that the directions lead somewhere different. The first type is then defined by an act, giving, rather than by a state of mind.

crossReferences.why: Completes the sorting this passage opens, giving three conditions for each type and a matched promise.
States the principle behind these oaths, that creation comes in pairs and the pairing is for thought.
Uses the same word for striving and attaches ownership to it rather than divergence.

studies.applyIt: Write down the three things you spent most of this week's energy on. Just the three, without ranking them. The ayah says efforts run in different directions, and most people have never actually looked at where theirs are pointing. Then leave the list somewhere you will see it on Friday.

studies.title: Giving, And Needing Nothing
studies.meaning: The turn sits in the second man's second verb. He withholds, which is common enough, and then he holds himself to be beyond need, which is the charge that actually lands. Commentators read that either as having no need of what giving would earn him or as having no need of God, and both readings are kept. Against him stands a man who gives and guards himself, and the two are then separated by what they do with something the surah names only as the most beautiful, leaving its noun unspoken.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Giving in the city was competitive and performed in public, and refusing was just as visible. Classical sources attach the closing lines of this surah to a wealthy believer who bought and freed people being persecuted for their faith, though the commentators observe that the wording stays general throughout and describes a type rather than naming anybody.

keyTerms.note: The root covers holding back what is expected of you. It is not a word about having little; it names a refusal at the moment of asking, which is why the verb that follows explains the attitude behind it.
A form meaning to seek or to claim independence. The object is left out, so the sentence can mean he felt no need of the reward or no need of God, and the ambiguity is not resolved.

A feminine superlative with its noun removed, so what is best is never said. Classical readings supply the promised reward, the word of God's oneness, or goodness itself, and the sources set them side by side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There was a loud kind of generosity in Mecca and a quiet one. The loud kind happened at gatherings, was counted, and turned into verse. The quiet kind was buying a person out of bondage or paying a fine for a man with no clan to stand behind him, and it bought the giver nothing at all socially, since the beneficiary had no standing to repay the gesture with reputation. The surah is describing the second kind.
studies.didYouKnow: The second half of this surah runs almost entirely on superlatives: the easiest way, the hardest, the most beautiful, the most wretched, the most God-fearing, the Most High. Arabic builds them all on a single pattern, so the sorting of people is carried out in a grammatical form that has no comfortable middle term available to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What is diagnosed is not stinginess but self-sufficiency, and the order of the verbs makes that explicit: the withholding comes first and is then explained by the attitude. The passage also refuses to treat giving as a transaction it can price. The man who gives is described by three things at once, only one of which involves money, and the other two are an inner caution and an act of assent.

crossReferences.why: Names the same disorder with the same verb, a person overstepping once he sees himself as needing nothing.
Promises that whoever is guarded from his own soul's grasping is among those who succeed.
Describes the fear of poverty as a suggestion whispered against giving, answered with a promise of bounty.

studies.applyIt: Give something small away today in a way that produces no acknowledgement: nobody knows it was you, nobody can thank you, nothing comes back. Then notice how much less satisfying it feels than the version where someone sees. That gap is the thing this passage is measuring.

studies.title: When The Money Cannot Reach
studies.meaning: A man falls, and the verb is one of tumbling into a pit rather than of dying in a bed, so the moment of need arrives at speed and his wealth is simply not there. Two statements follow in the same emphatic shape, one placing the guidance on God and one putting both worlds in His hands, the later world named before the earlier one. Then the voice changes. For the only time in the surah the speaker says I, and what He says is that He has warned them of a fire described by a verb of flaring rather than by any noun.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just sorted people into two kinds by what they do with their money and their assent; these lines close that argument by naming the things neither kind controls. Classical commentators mark the brief shift into the first person singular as unusual and read it as the warning being delivered directly rather than relayed. No specific occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: A verb of tumbling into a pit or down a slope, also used of perishing outright. It sets the moment of need at a fall, which is the one situation where nothing can be fetched in time.
The feminine for the earlier one, meaning the present world. Placing it after the hereafter reverses the order a listener expects and gathers both under a single ownership in one short line.
A verb rather than a description, from a root of flame licking upward. The fire is given as something doing rather than something being, which keeps it in the present tense of the warning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A trader's wealth travelled with him, roped onto the animals. The tracks out of Mecca ran along wadi beds and over ledges, and moving at night to avoid the heat meant moving where a misjudged step took a man and his packs over an edge together. Falls were the ordinary way that people and fortunes were lost on the road, which is why the image needed no elaboration for a first audience.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only line in the surah where God speaks as I. Everywhere else in these twenty-one ayat He is We, or He is spoken of in the third person, and the surrounding lines about guidance and ownership both use the plural. The singular appears once, for the warning, and then the surah returns to the plural and never uses it again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is stated as something resting on God rather than as something a person achieves, and the line immediately after removes every alternative address by putting both worlds under one owner. Together the two close off the escape the first line has just illustrated: there is nowhere outside the arrangement to fall to. The warning that follows is then delivered in the first person, so it arrives unmediated rather than as a report.

crossReferences.why: States the same responsibility in nearly the same construction, that the direction of the way rests upon God.
Says outright that wealth and children will not avail anyone at all against God on that day.
Shows the principle applied to one named man, whose wealth and earnings did nothing for him.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing you are quietly counting on to catch you if everything goes wrong: savings, a relative, a qualification, a person who owes you. You do not have to give it up or feel bad about it. Just say what it is out loud, once, and notice that you have one and that you had never named it.
